blocks.text: Annotation is the process of adding the labels, categories, or target outputs that turn raw, unlabeled examples into something a model can actually be trained on, whether that means tagging a support ticket with the right category or writing the ideal response to a given prompt.

For many fine-tuning projects, especially ones based on classification or extraction tasks, annotation is where the real bottleneck lives, since collecting raw examples is often far easier than producing accurate, consistent labels for them.
1. What Annotation Means in a Fine-Tuning Context

blocks.alt: An unlabeled example goes through annotation to become a labeled example

blocks.text: Annotation covers a wide range of activities, assigning a category label, marking which parts of a text are relevant, or writing out an ideal response, but the common thread is turning something raw into something a supervised training process can actually learn from.

Not every fine-tuning dataset requires heavy annotation, some tasks draw target outputs directly from existing records, but whenever a human judgment call is required, annotation quality tends to directly cap the ceiling on fine-tuned model quality.
2. Human Annotation, The Traditional Approach

blocks.alt: A human annotator applies a label to produce training data

blocks.text: Human annotation, whether performed by internal subject matter experts or an external annotation team, remains the most reliable source of high quality labels for tasks requiring genuine judgment, especially where mistakes are costly or the task is nuanced.

The tradeoff is cost and time, human annotation at scale is expensive and slow compared to automated alternatives, which is why later topics in this course also cover synthetic data generation as a complementary approach.
3. Writing Clear Annotation Guidelines

blocks.alt: Vague instructions are compared against clear guidelines

blocks.text: Annotation quality depends heavily on how clearly the task is defined for the people doing the labeling. Vague instructions, like label this as good or bad, produce inconsistent results, since different annotators will interpret good and bad differently.
Specific, example rich guidelines, with edge cases explicitly addressed, dramatically improve consistency, even though writing them well takes real upfront effort.

blocks.title: Edge cases deserve explicit examples
blocks.content: The clearest annotation guidelines usually include several worked edge case examples, since the boundary between categories is where most annotator disagreement actually happens.

blocks.text: 4. Inter-Annotator Agreement

blocks.alt: Annotator A and annotator B are checked against each other for agreement

blocks.text: A common quality check is having two or more annotators label the same subset of examples independently, then measuring how often they agree. Low agreement is a strong signal that the guidelines are unclear or the task itself is genuinely ambiguous.
High agreement, by contrast, is a reasonable signal that the labels are reliable enough to build a training dataset on.

code.content:
# A simplified agreement check between two annotators
matches = sum(1 for a, b in zip(labels_a, labels_b) if a == b)
agreement_rate = matches / len(labels_a)
if agreement_rate < 0.85:
    flag_for_guideline_review()

blocks.text: 5. Model Assisted Annotation

blocks.alt: A model drafts a label, a human reviews it, producing a confirmed label

blocks.text: A common way to speed up annotation is having a model produce a first draft label or response, which a human then reviews and corrects rather than writing from scratch, often significantly faster than pure manual annotation while keeping a human in the loop for quality.
This approach works best when the model draft is already reasonably close to correct most of the time, since reviewing and fixing a mostly right draft is faster than writing one from nothing.
6. Active Learning, Annotating What Matters Most

blocks.alt: Examples where the model is uncertain get prioritized for annotation

blocks.text: Active learning is a strategy where an existing model is used to identify which unlabeled examples it is least confident about, and those examples are prioritized for human annotation first, since they carry the most useful signal for improving the model.
This targets annotation effort toward the examples that actually move the needle, rather than spending equal effort labeling examples the model already handles well.
7. Quality Control Through Spot Checks

blocks.alt: A full annotated batch gets a spot check sample, confirming quality

blocks.text: Even with clear guidelines and agreement checks, ongoing spot checking, randomly sampling a portion of completed annotations for review, catches drift, an annotator gradually interpreting guidelines differently over time, or fatigue related errors on long batches.

blocks.text: 8. Annotation Tooling

Purpose built annotation tools, whether an off the shelf platform or a lightweight internal interface, make the annotation process faster and less error prone than working directly in a spreadsheet, particularly for tasks involving highlighting text spans or comparing multiple candidate responses.
Even a simple custom interface tailored to the exact task at hand often pays for the time invested building it through faster, more consistent annotation afterward.
9. Cost and Time Tradeoffs

Annotation cost scales with both the number of examples and the complexity of the judgment required per example, a simple binary label costs far less per item than writing a full, carefully considered response.

items: Simple categorical labels, fast to annotate, lower cost per example
Free text responses or nuanced judgments, slower to annotate, higher cost per example
Model assisted annotation, faster than pure manual annotation, still requires careful human review
Active learning, reduces total annotation volume needed by targeting the most informative examples

blocks.text: Worked Example

A team needs ten thousand support tickets labeled with one of twelve issue categories. Pure manual annotation of all ten thousand would take weeks, so they instead have a model draft a category for every ticket, then have annotators review and correct only the drafts.

They measure inter-annotator agreement on a shared sample early on, discover confusion between two similar categories, revise the guidelines with explicit examples distinguishing them, and see agreement improve significantly on a follow up sample before proceeding with the full batch.
Common Mistakes

items: Writing vague annotation guidelines and being surprised when different annotators disagree
Skipping an inter-annotator agreement check and only discovering inconsistent labels after training
Trusting model assisted draft labels without meaningful human review
Spending equal annotation effort across all examples instead of prioritizing the ones a model is least confident about

blocks.text: Practice

Write a one paragraph annotation guideline for a labeling task you have in mind, then hand it to someone else and ask them to label five examples using only your written instructions, noting where their interpretation differs from what you intended.
Key Takeaway

Annotation turns raw examples into usable training signal, and its quality depends on clear guidelines, measured agreement between annotators, and ongoing spot checks, with model assisted annotation and active learning offering practical ways to reduce cost without sacrificing that quality.
